name: GROW Model
use_case: Staff keep bringing their problems to their manager, who simply tells them what to do, so they never learn to work things out themselves; one-to-one meetings and staff appraisal conversations drift and end without a clear agreement. Instead of advising, the manager asks a short sequence of questions: what the employee wants, where things stand, what they could do, and what they will do by when. The employee leaves with their own solution and a dated next step.
strengths: simple enough to learn in an hour and to keep in mind during a live conversation
shifts the leader from supplying answers to asking questions, so ownership of the solution stays with the other person
the closing commitment stage turns a pleasant talk into a named action, a date and a way to check back
fits a 20-minute check-in as well as a longer development conversation
widely taught in public services, health care and schools, so many staff will already recognise it
weaknesses: only works if the person has, or can find, the knowledge needed; it cannot replace teaching or instruction
the power gap between a line manager and a direct report can make questions feel like a test rather than an invitation
easily reduced to reading out a fixed list of questions in order, which feels scripted and closes down thinking
goal-centred by design, so it gives little room for open-ended exploration of values, identity or meaning
most published guidance is practitioner and training material; few studies test the four-stage structure separately from coaching in general
use_cases: A head teacher notices that teachers come to her door with every classroom difficulty and leave with her solution, and she wants her next one-to-one talks to help them work out their own way forward instead.
Annual staff development talks in a municipal department run through the same form every year, drift into general chat and end without anyone agreeing what the employee will actually do next.

A clinical supervisor has a trainee who is stuck on a recurring difficulty with a patient group and wants a short, structured conversation that ends with the trainee's own action plan rather than the supervisor's advice.
A newly promoted team lead in a nonprofit wants a simple way to run regular check-ins that leave each volunteer coordinator with one clear commitment and a date to review it.
Someone facing a career decision wants to think it through on their own or with a peer, starting from what they want and ending with a first step they will take this month.
